title: Per-customer fencing and reconciliation sweep for transient retry billing correctness
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: We see classes of transient failures (HTTP timeouts, connection resets, consumer restarts) where clients retry 'at-least-once' and the serving runtime ingests overlapping partial outputs from the same logical operation. Current meters count per-token consumption when persisted from the serving tier, and some partial retries result in double consumption for the same logical user intent. Existing nonces/replay tokens catch some cases, but they fail when clients split requests across multiple small sub-requests (partial-batch retries) or when retries cross RPC boundaries (e.g., resumed streams).

Goal: Implement a per-customer fencing mechanism combined with an asynchronous reconciliation sweep to ensure eventual billing correctness for transient partial-batch retries, while keeping tail latency and throughput stable. The system must: 1) prevent immediate double-counting at ingest time for obvious retried sequences, 2) detect and correct edge cases where duplicated meter writes occur after the fact, and 3) provide observability and an audit trail for any adjustments.

Non-goals: This ticket does not cover upstream SDK changes for new retry patterns (those will be handled in a separate SDK upgrade RFC) and does not attempt to be a full replacement for the existing global-nonce strategy. It augments current defenses with a tenant-scoped fencing and reconciliation layer targeted at partial-batch semantics.

Design summary: 
- Fencing token (fence_id): when a customer opens a logical operation (chat session or batch generation), the gateway issues a short-lived per-customer fence_id and a monotonically-incrementing sequence number (session_seq) embedded in every ingest record. Fence_ids are rotated on session boundaries and after long inactivity.
- Fast-path checks: On ingest, the meter-write path checks (customer_id, fence_id, session_seq) for a recent identical or higher session_seq; identical seq => idempotent accept (no new charge), lower seq => drop (duplicate), higher seq => accept. This provides immediate dedupe for the common retry pattern without blocking serving.
- Reconciliation sweep: For cases where duplicate consumption still gets persisted (e.g., when session_seq wasn't present or client resumed without fence), an async reconciler job runs periodic sweeps over the recent time window (configurable, default 48h) and uses heuristics to group likely-duplicate consumption footprints (same customer, correlated request fingerprints, overlapping KV cache keys, coalesced timestamp ranges). The reconciler emits ledger corrections (negative adjustments) and writes audit events to an immutable corrections table.
- Safe windows and SLA: To avoid accidental refunds for legitimate concurrent requests, we use conservative heuristics with thresholds (token overlap > 70% and similarity score > 0.85) and require correlating trace IDs or matching prompt hashes where available. Reconciler runs behind feature flags and is limited to customers who opt-in during Canary.
- Exposure in Console: Add a "Billing Reconciliation" dashboard with counts of reconciliations, total adjusted tokens, top impacted customers, and RCA links. Provide an API to fetch correction events for a customer for transparency and dispute handling.

Implementation milestones: 
1) schema and ingest tag support (DB + proto): add fence_id and session_seq to ingest proto and ledger rows; DB migration with backfill markers.
2) fast-path ingest checks: lightweight index on (customer_id, fence_id, session_seq) with TTL; deterministic accept/drop logic runnable inline in the write path.
3) reconciler job: implement sweep service in Go, idempotent commit protocol for applying negative ledger entries, and instrumentation.
4) admin APIs + console surfaces: expose reconciliation events and correction totals; feature flag controls.
5) Canary rollout and rollback plan.

Metrics / success criteria: 
- 95% reduction in immediate duplicate ingestion events for retried sessions in canary customers.
- Reconciler correctness: false-positive correction rate < 0.1% on canary customers (verified by manual audit).
- No more than 2% p99 tail latency regression on ingest path after fast-path checks enabled.

Rollout plan: 
- Phase 0 (dev): unit tests, integration tests, and canary reconciler runs against staging dataset.
- Phase 1 (internal canary): enable ingest fast-path checks behind FF for internal accounts and run reconciler in dry-run mode (generate corrections but do not apply).
- Phase 2 (customer canary): invite 5-10 low-risk customers to opt-in; enable real reconciler corrections with manual approval and human-in-the-loop for first 48h.
- Phase 3: scale to all customers with dynamic thresholds and automated QA.
- Rollback: disable reconciler application via FF and issue compensating edits if necessary (we keep an immutable corrections table for audit and reversal).

Open questions / risks: 
- SDK adoption: clients that do not send session_seq will fall back to reconciler-only protection; reconcile-only coverage must be robust.
- Cost of reconciler: scanning and heuristic comparisons are CPU-intensive; need to estimate cost and cap per-tenant.
- Edge-case concurrency: simultaneous legitimate parallel requests that share a prompt may be misclassified; we aim to reduce this via stricter similarity thresholds and requiring multiple signals.

acceptance_criteria: Ingest path accepts session_seq and fence_id; schema migration completed and backward compatible
Fast-path dedupe check implemented with unit and integration tests; p99 ingest latency regression < 2%
Reconciler job runs in dry-run and produces candidate corrections for staging dataset
Console shows reconciliation metrics and exposes per-customer correction history API
Canary customer run with manual approval demonstrates false-positive correction rate < 0.1%
